newsitem.title: USA: U.S. study gauges risks to brain from heart surgery.
newsitem.headline: U.S. study gauges risks to brain from heart surgery.

text.p: People who undergo heart bypass surgery may face a far higher risk of a stroke than previous estimates have suggested, according to a study in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.

Doctors who analyzed records from 24 U.S. medical centers found that the operation leads to a stroke or fatal brain injury in about three percent of the cases and another three percent have seizures, memory problems or a lower IQ.

Past studies have suggested that the risks were as much as 10 times lower. Stroke is the third leading cause of death in the United States, according to the Ischemia Research and Education Foundation, which underwrote the latest study.

The research involved 2,108 patients and is significant because more than 800,000 people throughout the world undergo some type of bypass surgery each year in hopes of reopening clogged arteries. Doctors have long known that these patients seemed to face a higher risk of stroke or other brain-related complications but the size of the risk has been disputed.

Dr. Dennis Mangano, one of the chief investigators in the new study, said the rate it found "may be just the tip of the iceberg" because it does not count minor problems with memory and concentration seen in an estimated 25 to 75 percent of bypass surgery patients during their hospital stays.

Led by Dr. Gary Roach of Kaiser Permanente Medical Center in San Francisco, the group also analyzed the 2,108 cases in hopes of finding warning signs doctors might heed to reduce the risk. They found a greater likelihood of stroke or some other brain-related complication following the heart surgery in patients with fatty deposits lining the major artery leading out of the heart, a history of neurological problems, high blood pressure, alcohol abuse or lung problems.
Roach suggested that if doctors carefully check the major artery -- the aorta -- "we may be able to immediately reduce the number of strokes following coronary bypass surgery."

When aorta-related strokes occur, it may be because the surgical clamps that close off the aorta have dislodged a fatty deposit, which can travel to the brain and block the flow of blood, causing a stroke.
The team said doctors need "new diagnostic and therapeutic strategies" to cut the risk of stroke after bypass surgery.
